'''David George Haskell''' is a British and American biologist and writer. He is a two-time [[Pulitzer Prize]] finalist in General Nonfiction. In addition to scientific papers, he has written essays, poems, op-eds,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Haskell |first=David George |date=29 March 2013 |title=Nature's Case for Same-Sex Marriage |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/03/30/opinion/natures-case-for-same-sex-marriage.html |url-access=subscription |department=Opinion |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> and the books ''[[The Forest Unseen]]'' ([[Viking Press]], [[Penguin Random House]] 2012), ''The Songs of Trees'' ([[Viking Press]], [[Penguin Random House]] 2017), ''Thirteen Ways to Smell a Tree'' ([[Hachette Book Group|Hachette]] 2021), and ''Sounds Wild and Broken'' ([[Viking Press]], [[Penguin Random House]] 2022). In 2026, [[Viking Press]] published ''How Flowers Made Our World: The Story of Nature's Revolutionaries''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Haskell |first=David George |date=24 March 2026 |title=How Flowers Made Our World: The Story of Nature's Revolutionaries |url=https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/775876/how-flowers-made-our-world-by-david-george-haskell |edition=First hardcover |location=New York |publisher=Viking |isbn=9780593834961 |oclc=1561100924 |access-date=28 March 2026}} {{Google books|id=kSt4EQAAQBAJ|title=How Flowers Made Our World}}.</ref>

==Education and academic appointments==
Haskell received his B.A. in zoology from the [[University of Oxford]] and his Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from [[Cornell University]]. His primary and secondary education were at l'[[École Jeannine Manuel|École Active Bilingue (now named École Jeannine Manuel]]), Paris, and the [[British School of Paris]], France. 

In 2025, he was appointed Adjunct Professor in the Department of Environmental Sciences at [[Emory University]] in Atlanta, Georgia. He was professor at [[Sewanee: The University of the South|The University of the South]] from 1995 to 2025, serving as Chair of Biology (2004–2009) and Director of Environmental Arts and Humanities (2024–2025), William R. Kenan, Jr. Professor of Biology and Environmental Studies (2021–2025), and Professor Emeritus of Biology (2025 onward).  In 2020–2021, he was Professor Adjunct in the Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology at the [[University of Colorado Boulder|University of Colorado, Boulder]].

==Work==
''[[The Forest Unseen|The Forest Unseen: A Year's Watch in Nature]]'' was winner of the 2013 [[National Academies Communication Award]] for Best Book,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=09052013A|title=Academies Announce 2013 Communication Award Winners|publisher=The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |date=September 5, 2013}}</ref> finalist for the [[2013 Pulitzer Prize]] in General Nonfiction,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pulitzer.org/citation/2013-General-Nonfiction|title=2013 Pulitzer Prizes|publisher=The Pulitzer Prizes|access-date=December 5, 2016}}</ref> runner-up for the 2013 [[PEN/E. O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pen.org/literature/2013-pene-o-wilson-literary-science-writing-award|title=2013 PEN/E. O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award |date=25 July 2013 |publisher=PEN America|access-date=December 5, 2016}}</ref> winner of the 2012 [[National Outdoor Book Award]] for Natural History Literature, and the 2013 Reed Environmental Writing Award.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.southernenvironment.org/projects/reed-environmental-writing-award|title=Reed Environmental Writing Award |publisher=Southern Environmental Law Center|access-date=December 5, 2016}}</ref> Biologist [[E. O. Wilson]] wrote that the book was "…a new genre of nature writing, located between science and poetry".<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Forest Unseen: A Year's Watch in Nature by David George Haskell |url=https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/309637/the-forest-unseen-by-david-george-haskell/|access-date=2022-01-20 |website=Penguin Random House |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Outside (magazine)|Outside Magazine]] listed the book among those that "shaped the decade", stating that it "injects much-needed vibrancy into the stuffy world of nature writing".<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-12-25|title=The Outdoor Books that Shaped the Last Decade|url=https://www.outsideonline.com/culture/books-media/best-outdoor-adventure-health-books-2010s/|access-date=2022-01-20|website=Outside Online|language=en-US}}</ref> ''The Forest Unseen'' has been translated into twelve languages and was winner, in translation, of the 2016 Dapeng Nature Book Award in China.

''The Songs of Trees: Stories from Nature's Great Connectors'', was published in April 2017 by Viking. It won the 2018 [[John Burroughs Medal]] for Distinguished Natural History Writing<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.johnburroughsassociation.org/component/zoo/item/david-haskell-wins-2018-burroughs-medal|title=DAVID HASKELL WINS 2018 BURROUGHS MEDAL |publisher=John Burroughs Association|access-date=March 12, 2018}}</ref> and the Iris Books Award.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bloomington|first=Inside IU|date=2020-01-27|title=Around IU Bloomington|url=https://news.iu.edu/stories/2020/01/iub/inside/28-news-roundup.html|access-date=2022-01-20|website=News at IU|language=en}}</ref> Jurors for the Iris Award called ''The Songs of Trees'' "a compelling example of poetic science" that "beautifully illustrates the interconnections … of particular trees around the world, weaving together scientific knowledge about them and their relationships to the rest of the natural world including humans."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Iris Book Award: Religion, Science, and Technology: Projects: Center for Religion & the HumanA research center of the Office of the Vice Provost for Research, Indiana University Bloomington: Indiana University|url=https://crh.indiana.edu/projects/religion-science-technology/iris-book-award.html|access-date=2022-01-20|website=Center for Religion & the HumanA research center of the Office of the Vice Provost for Research, Indiana University Bloomington|language=en-US}}</ref> [[Public Radio International]]'s [[Science Friday]] named ''The Songs of Trees'' of the Best Science Books of 2017,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencefriday.com/segments/the-best-science-books-of-2017/|title=The Best Science Books Of 2017|publisher=Science Friday, PRI|access-date=March 12, 2018}}</ref> [[Maria Popova]] included the book in [[Brain Pickings]] Favorite Science Books of 2017, writing that Haskell is "the rare kind of scientist Rachel Carson was when long ago she pioneered a new cultural aesthetic of poetic prose about science",<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.brainpickings.org/2017/12/13/best-science-books-2017/|title=7 Favorite Science Books of 2017|date=13 December 2017 |publisher=Brain Pickings|access-date=March 12, 2018}}</ref> and [[Forbes.com]] named the book one of 10 Best Environment, Climate Science and Conservation Books of 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/grrlscientist/2018/01/26/the-10-best-environment-climate-science-and-conservation-books-of-2017/|title=The 10 Best Environment, Climate Science and Conservation Books of 2017|work=forbes.com|access-date=March 12, 2018}}</ref> ''The Songs of Trees'' has been translated into fourteen languages.

''Sounds Wild and Broken'' (Viking, 2022) was a finalist for the [[Pulitzer Prize]] in General Nonfiction.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Khatib |first1=Joumana |last2=Alter |first2=Alexandra |last3=Harris |first3=Elizabeth A. |title=Pulitzer Prizes 2023: A Guide to the Winning Books and Finalists |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 8, 2023 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/05/08/books/pulitzer-prize-books-winners-finalists.html|access-date=May 16, 2023 |language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|df=mdy-all }}</ref> It was also a Finalist for the 2023 [[PEN America|PEN]]/ E. O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award and an Editor's Choice and a Recommended Paperback in the ''New York Times'' book review.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-03-31 |title=10 New Books We Recommend This Week |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/31/books/review/10-new-books-we-recommend-this-week.html |access-date=2022-04-01 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Salazar |first=Miguel |date=2023-04-14 |title=6 New Paperbacks to Read This Week |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/04/14/books/review/new-paperbacks-jefferson.html |access-date=2023-04-23 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> [[Cynthia Barnett]] reviewing in ''[[The New York Times]]'', wrote of the book that it "affirms Haskell as a laureate for the earth".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barnett |first=Cynthia |date=2022-03-05 |title=Crescendos of Crickets and Choruses of Frogs |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/05/books/review/crescendos-of-crickets-and-choruses-of-frogs.html |access-date=2022-03-28 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The  [[Acoustical Society of America]] awarded the book its 2021-2 Science Communication Award, Long Form Print.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-21 |title=Science Writing Awards 2021-2022 |url=https://acoustics.org/science-writing-awards-2021-2022/ |access-date=2024-02-27 |language=en-US}}</ref> 

''Thirteen Ways to Smell a Tree'' was described by Sir [[Peter Crane]], FRS, as "'eclectic, brilliant and beautifully written" and by [[Kate Humble]] in [[Radio Times|The Radio Times]] Best Books of 2021 as "My favourite book of the year".

In ''The New York Times Book Review'',<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nicolson|first=Adam|date=March 25, 2026|title=A Passionate Floral Manifesto |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/25/books/review/how-flowers-made-our-world-david-george-haskell.html |access-date=2026-05-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> author [[Adam Nicolson]] said of ''How Flowers Made Our World,'' "A work of real passion… You feel like cheering. More Haskells, please, and more flowers". Christoph Irmscher wrote of the book in ''The Wall Street Journal'', "exuberant prose engages all our senses, beckoning us, the way a flower would a curious bee, into a world of hidden wonders."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Irmscher |first=Christoph |date=2026-04-17 |title=‘How Flowers Made Our World’ Review: The Blooms That Boomed |url=https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/how-flowers-made-our-world-review-the-blooms-that-boomed-39809825 |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=The Wall Street Journal |language=en-US}}</ref>

Journalist Paul Kvinta's profile of Haskell<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-03-23|title=David Haskell Speaks for the Trees|url=https://www.outsideonline.com/culture/books-media/david-haskell-speaks-trees/|access-date=2022-01-23|website=Outside Online|language=en-US}}</ref> in [[Outside (magazine)|''Outside'']] magazine was included in the 2018 anthology [[The Best American Science and Nature Writing|Best American Science and Nature Writing]], edited by [[Sam Kean]].

He served on the jury for the 2026 [[Pulitzer Prize]] in General Nonfiction<ref>{{Cite web |title=General Nonfiction {{!}} The Pulitzer Prizes |url=https://www.pulitzer.org/prize-winners-by-category/223 |access-date=2026-05-19 |website=www.pulitzer.org |language=en}}</ref>, alongside [[Luis Alberto Urrea]] (chair), [[Marcia Chatelain]], [[Andrea Elliott]], and [[David Greenberg (historian)|David Greenberg]].

* Finalist, [[PEN America]]/E. O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award. 2023.

* Patricia Winn Award for Southern Literature. 2023.
* Winner (Gold and Listener’s Choice), Signal Awards for three categories: “Most Innovative Audio Experience,” “Best Editing,” and “Best Sound Design” (for “When the Earth Started to Sing” published with collaborators in Emergence Magazine). January 2023.
* Iris Book Award for outstanding writing in science, religion, and nature. 2020.
* Ping Shan Natural History Book Award, China. 2020.
* Social Impact Media Awards: Best VR Experience and Jury Prizes for Immersive Impact and Journalistic Achievement. For The Atomic Tree, directed by E. Vaughan-Lee and A. Loften, script D. Haskell, E. Vaughn-Lee, and A Loften. 2020.

* China Times Open Book Awards: The Best Book for Life. Taiwan. 2017.
* Dapeng Nature Writing Award. Shenzhen, China. 2016.
* [[Guggenheim Fellowship|John Simon Guggenheim Fellowship]]. 2014-2015.
* [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|National Academies]]’ 2013 Communication Award for Best Book. (Given by the National Academy of Sciences, National Academy of Engineering, and Institute of Medicine, with support from the Keck Foundation.)
* Finalist for 2013 [[Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction]].
* Winner of the 2013 Reed Environmental Writing Award.
* Winner of the 2012 [[National Outdoor Book Award]] for Natural History Literature.
* Runner-up for 2013 [[PEN America]]/E. O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award.
Other awards:

In 2009 he was named the [[Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching|Carnegie]]-[[Council for Advancement and Support of Education|CASE]] Professor of the Year in Tennessee.<ref>{{cite news|title=David Haskell named Tennessee's top professor|url=http://news-archive.sewanee.edu/people/2009/11/18/david-haskell-named-tennessees-top-professor|work=Sewanee Today|publisher=Sewanee: The University of the South|date=November 18, 2009|archive-date=February 5, 2017|access-date=December 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170205100518/http://news-archive.sewanee.edu/people/2009/11/18/david-haskell-named-tennessees-top-professor|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] by the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]] in 2014.<ref>{{cite web|title=David Haskell|url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/david-haskell/|publisher=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation|access-date=December 5, 2016}}</ref>

In 2022, Haskell was elected a fellow of the [[Linnean Society of London]]. He is also a fellow of the [[American Council of Learned Societies]] and elected member of the [[American Ornithological Society]].

== Support of conservation and environmental justice organizations ==
In the Acknowledgments section of ''The Forest Unseen'', Haskell writes that "I will donate at least half my author's proceeds to projects that benefit forest conservation". In the same section of ''Sounds Wild and Broken'', he states "In these pages, I make the case that the acoustic crisis has four main pressing and intersecting dimensions...loss of ecological habitat and attacks on human rights...the nightmare of industrial sound in the oceans...the inequities of noise pollution in cities...failures to listen to and celebrate the storied sensory richness of our world. I will donate at lest half of my net proceeds from this book to organizations that work to heal and reverse these aggressions, fragmentations, and loses." He donated to education and conservation groups all of his proceeds from the sale of the best-selling ''Eastern Forest Playing Cards'' with the Art of Play.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eastern Forest Playing Cards |url=https://www.artofplay.com/products/eastern-forest-playing-cards |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=Art of Play |language=en}}</ref>

Haskell served on advisory boards for the [[Open Space Institute]] and as board member and leader of the Shakerag Hollow Conservation Initiative for the South Cumberland Regional Land Trust. He serves on the advisory board of Advisory Board, MAX (Media Art Exploration).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-30 |title=Media Art Xploration |url=https://mediaartexploration.org/ |access-date=2024-08-08 |language=en-US}}</ref>
